individuel.explanation: "Individuel" means "individual". It comes from the noun "et individ" (an individual person). To describe a talk that is meant for just one person, put it before the noun: "en individuel samtale" (an individual conversation).

indlysende.explanation: "Indlysende" means "obvious". To say that a fact is clear to everyone, use it after "Det er": "Det er indlysende, at han tager fejl" (It is obvious that he is wrong).

indre.explanation: "Indre" means "inner". To talk about the central part of a city, say "den indre by" (the inner city). To talk about feelings inside a person, say "indre uro" (inner unrest).

indsigt.explanation: "En indsigt" means "an insight". To say what a person understands well, put "i" (in) after it: "Hun har god indsigt i økonomi" (She has good insight into economics).

indtil.explanation: "Indtil" means "until". To say when something stops, put a time after it: "indtil fredag" (until Friday). To say something lasts until an event happens, put a whole sentence after it: "Bliv, indtil du er rask" (Stay until you are well).

indtil nu.explanation: "Indtil nu" means "until now". It is built from "indtil" (until) and "nu" (now). To talk about what happens from this moment forward, use "fra nu af" (from now on): "Fra nu af kommer jeg i tide" (From now on I will be on time).

indtil videre.explanation: "Indtil videre" means "so far". It is built from "indtil" (until) and "videre" (further). To talk about the coming days, it means "for now": "Vi holder lukket indtil videre" (We are staying closed for now).

indviklet.explanation: "Indviklet" means "complicated". It comes from the verb "at indvikle" (to wrap up), so something "indviklet" is wrapped up in itself and hard to follow.

ineffektiv.explanation: "Ineffektiv" means "inefficient". It is built from "effektiv" (efficient) with "in" in front, which turns it into the opposite. To say that a medicine does not give the result you want, use it for the medicine: "en ineffektiv medicin" (an ineffective medicine).

inficeret.explanation: "Inficeret" means "infected". It comes from the verb "at inficere" (to infect). To say that a person has caught an illness, use "smittet" (infected) instead: "Han er smittet" (He is infected).

inflation.explanation: "Inflation" means "inflation". To say that prices are going up, use the verb "at stige" (to rise): "Inflationen stiger" (Inflation is rising).

influenza.explanation: "Influenza" means "flu". To say you have the flu, leave out "en" (a): "Jeg har influenza" (I have the flu).

information.explanation: "Information" means "information". To say what the information is about, put "om" (about) after it: "information om togene" (information about the trains).

informeret.explanation: "Informeret" means "informed". It comes from the verb "at informere" (to inform). To name the topic you know about, use "om" (about): "Er du informeret om ændringen?" (Are you informed about the change?)

ingefær.explanation: "Ingefær" means "ginger". To name a drink made with ginger, put "ingefær" in front of the drink: "ingefærte" (ginger tea) and "ingefærøl" (ginger beer).

ingen.explanation: "Ingen" means "no one". To say you have none of something, use it before the noun, as "no": "Der er ingen billetter" (There are no tickets). Danish does not add "ikke" (not) next to it, so say "Jeg kender ingen her" (I know no one here). In a question, use "nogen" (anyone) instead: "Er der nogen hjemme?" (Is anyone home?)

ingen problemer.explanation: "Ingen problemer" means "no problem". To agree when someone asks you for a small favor, say it as your answer: "Kan jeg få en pose?" "Ingen problemer." (Can I have a bag? No problem.) A longer way to say the same is "Det er ikke noget problem" (That is not a problem).

ingen årsag.explanation: "Ingen årsag" means "don't mention it". Literally, it says "no reason". To answer when someone thanks you, say it as your reply: "Tak for lånet." "Ingen årsag." (Thanks for the loan. Don't mention it.)

ingenting.explanation: "Ingenting" means "nothing". To say you see something, use "noget" (something): "Jeg ser noget" (I see something). Danish does not add "ikke" (not) next to "ingenting", so say "Jeg ved ingenting" (I know nothing). To say that no person is there, use "ingen" (no one): "Ingen er her" (No one is here).

inklusive.explanation: "Inklusive" means "including". To list what a price covers, put it before the item: "inklusive fragt" (including shipping). It can also come after the item: "Morgenmad inklusive" (Breakfast included).

inspireret.explanation: "Inspireret" means "inspired". To name the person or thing that inspired you, add "af" (by) after it: "inspireret af en bog" (inspired by a book).

intakt.explanation: "Intakt" means "intact". English speakers should spell it with "kt" at the end, not "ct". To say a delivered package is not damaged, say: "Pakken er intakt" (The package is intact).

intelligens.explanation: "En intelligens" means "an intelligence". It is the noun for the describing word "intelligent" (intelligent).

intelligent.explanation: "Intelligent" means "intelligent". It is the describing word for the noun "intelligens" (intelligence). To say an animal shows good thinking, use it before the noun: "en intelligent hund" (an intelligent dog).

interessant.explanation: "Interessant" means "interesting". To say something sounds interesting, use "lyder" (sounds): "Det lyder interessant" (That sounds interesting). To say you are interested, use "interesseret" (interested) instead: "Jeg er interesseret i musik" (I am interested in music).
